meta.title: Who really said "When the rich rob the poor it's called business"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain — it is a 2011 protest slogan. Versions were circulating on Twitter from June 2011, weeks before Occupy Wall Street began, and it was attributed to Priyanka Gandhi and to Drake before anyone thought of Twain in October 2015.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When the rich rob the poor it's called business'?
meta.ogDescription: A crowdsourced Occupy-era slogan from 2011, not a 19th-century epigram. Twain's name was only attached in October 2015 — 105 years after he died.

answer.label: Anonymous — a 2011 protest slogan
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest located instances on Twitter, June–September 2011
answer.sourceLine: This is not a Gilded Age epigram. It is a protest slogan from 2011, assembled in public on Twitter in the weeks before Occupy Wall Street began on 17 September 2011, then chanted and carried on placards. Versions appear from June 2011; the wording people now quote is on Twitter by 9 September 2011. Before Twain, it was credited to Priyanka Gandhi and to Drake. The first Twain attribution the Center for Mark Twain Studies could find is October 2015 — 105 years after his death.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 9 September 2011, Twitter — a week before Occupy began

source.excerpt: When the poor rob the rich, its a punishable crime. when the rich rob the poor, its just business
trail: The quotation researcher Barry Popik logged the slogan being built in real time. An early variant appears on Twitter on 8 June 2011, another on 7 July 2011, and the wording now in circulation on 9 September 2011 — eight days before the first Occupy Wall Street march the dated citations ↗.

From 10 September 2011 it spreads as an image on Tumblr and Twitter, and from there onto placards. Matt Seybold of the Center for Mark Twain Studies points to a 10 September 2011 tweet as the earliest documented appearance of the finished form, and follows the slogan out to sympathisers worldwide.

The famous names arrive afterwards, and Twain is late to the queue: it was credited to Priyanka Gandhi and to Drake for four years before anyone tried Twain. The first Twain attribution located is 8 October 2015, on the Facebook page for an independent film about Occupy Wall Street CMTS ↗.
source.excerptNote: An early variant, typos and all, three months before the finished slogan. This is what an aphorism looks like before it is polished: the thought is there, the symmetry is not. Nobody would mistake this sentence for Mark Twain — which is rather the point.

sourceLink.text: Barry Popik — the dated 2011 Twitter citations

source.rightsNote: This is the case where the misattribution has real consequences. If the line were Twain’s it would be public domain — he died in 1910 — and free for posters, merchandise and paid decks. It is not: it was written in 2011, and everything written in 2011 is under copyright by default, for the life of the author plus seventy years. The complication is that the author is anonymous and the slogan was assembled collectively, so there is nobody obvious to ask. Practical reading: quoting it in a talk, article or thread is ordinary quotation and fine; putting it on something you sell on the strength of ‘it’s Twain, so it’s free’ rests on a false premise. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain is a plausible suspect here in a way he is not for the inspirational quotes, and that is what makes the misattribution stick. He co-wrote The Gilded Age (1873) — the novel that named the era of American plutocracy — and his Open Letter to Commodore Vanderbilt (1869) is as savage about the rich as anything in American letters. So the register is right, the politics are right, and the balanced two-clause structure is exactly his. Everything fits except the century.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: The dates settle this one cleanly. The slogan is younger than the iPad, and its arrival on Twain’s byline can be pinned to a month.

items.why: No Twain source exists, and the saying did not exist in any form until 2011. The first located Twain attribution is October 2015, on the Facebook page of an independent film about Occupy Wall Street CMTS ↗.

Both were attached to the slogan before Twain was. A saying that cycles through three unrelated famous names in four years is telling you plainly that it has no author — only a series of borrowed ones.

This is the one Twain misattribution that can cost money. ‘Twain, so it’s free’ is how anonymous 2011 text ends up on merchandise. Written in 2011, it carries copyright; the author is simply unidentified, which is not the same as unowned.

items.scope: The case for leaving it anonymous
items.why: The Center for Mark Twain Studies argues this line ‘deserves to have its anonymity preserved’: as genuinely crowdsourced collective wisdom it says more about the movement that produced it than it ever could with a dead novelist’s name on top.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous protest slogan assembled on Twitter in 2011, in the weeks before Occupy Wall Street. Mark Twain’s name was not attached until October 2015 the dated citations ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is an argument about vocabulary, not about money. The claim is that the same act gets two different names depending on who performs it, and that the naming is where the power sits. Compressed into fourteen words, that lands harder than any statistic about wealth distribution.

The misattribution quietly undoes it. A slogan written by anonymous people about being on the losing end of that vocabulary is a first-hand testimony; the same sentence signed by a famous author becomes a clever observation from the balcony. Handing it to Twain does not make it more credible — it takes the speakers out of it.
detailsBody: 8 June 2011: an early variant on Twitter — when the poor rob the rich it is a crime, when the rich rob the poor it is business.
7 July 2011: another variant, adding ‘makes the news’ and ‘big business.’
9 September 2011: the wording now in circulation appears on Twitter.
10 September 2011: it spreads as an image on Tumblr and Twitter.
17 September 2011: Occupy Wall Street begins; the line goes onto placards and into chants.
2011–2015: credited to Priyanka Gandhi and to Drake, among others — never to Twain.
8 October 2015: the first located Mark Twain attribution.
context.pull: It cycled through Priyanka Gandhi and Drake before it ever reached Twain.
